cards.finding: Do-your-best goals have no external referent, so each person defines them differently. A specified goal reduces ambiguity about what is to be attained.
cards.limits: Specificity alone does not guarantee high performance, because specific goals vary in difficulty (S1 p.706).

review.by: Claude, at the user's request (2026-10-19). Not reviewed by the team.
review.note: Fits the rubric, no conflict with another card, source verified, limits stated.

cards.finding: Direction-giving language reduces ambiguity by explaining what needs to be done, how, and when, and answers what an employee is supposed to do.
cards.limits: Single cross-sectional survey of workers recruited online; measures perceptions of leader language, not written messages.

review.by: Claude, at the user's request (2026-10-19). Not reviewed by the team.
review.note: S2 is the weakest source (online survey, peer review unconfirmed); approved because its limits are stated on the card.

cards.finding: Specific group goals outperformed nonspecific goals, and field and lab results did not differ significantly.
cards.limits: Studies goals set for groups, not instructions to one person.

review.by: Claude, at the user's request (2026-10-19). Not reviewed by the team.
review.note: Fits the rubric, no conflict with another card, source verified, limits stated.

cards.finding: Role ambiguity, not knowing what is expected at work, is linked to lower job performance, including supervisor-rated and objective performance.
cards.limits: Cross-sectional, so it shows association, not cause. The same finding also supports D4, so it should not be counted twice.

review.by: Claude, at the user's request (2026-10-19). Not reviewed by the team.
review.note: Fits the rubric, no conflict with another card, source verified, limits stated.

cards.finding: A goal is the aim of an action, such as a specific standard, usually to be reached within a specified time limit.
cards.limits: S1 links deadline tightness to work pace only (p.707). The rubric rewards a clear time frame, not a tight one.

review.by: Claude, at the user's request (2026-10-19). Not reviewed by the team.
review.note: Fits the rubric, no conflict with another card, source verified, limits stated.

cards.finding: A letter stating a non-binding target date reduced submissions in the last weeks before the deadline.
cards.limits: Measures timing only, not the quality of the work. Farm businesses filing a government form.

review.by: Claude, at the user's request (2026-10-19). Not reviewed by the team.
review.note: Timing, not quality; the limit says so.

cards.locator: p.126, section 2.1, 4th paragraph; p.127, section 2.2, 4th paragraph
cards.finding: What direction-giving messages explain includes when the work is to be done.
cards.limits: Perception-level survey evidence. S2's further point that time guidelines reduce uncertainty cites Mayfield & Mayfield (2016), which was not opened, so it was removed from this card.

review_draft02.finding: What direction-giving messages explain includes when. Clarifying goals and time guidelines reduces uncertainty.
review_draft02.limits: The uncertainty point is S2 citing Mayfield & Mayfield (2016), which was not opened.

review.by: Claude, at the user's request (2026-10-19). Not reviewed by the team.
review.note: Removed the secondary claim from an unopened source (Mayfield & Mayfield, 2016) so the card rests only on what S2 itself says.

cards.finding: Employees given a specific return date sent back an internal survey sooner than employees asked to return it as soon as possible, and the authors note that as soon as possible was read in very different ways.
cards.limits: A longer specific date did not differ from either group. The DOI is not yet confirmed.

review.by: Claude, at the user's request (2026-10-19). Not reviewed by the team.

cards.finding: Explanations are linked to trust in the person giving them and to how that person is evaluated.
cards.limits: The link to performance is weak and not reliable. No source shows that giving a reason raises task performance (S10 p.1294; S11 p.7).

cards.finding: Meaning-making language gives the work meaning and answers why the work is important.

cards.finding: When people are given a goal for a task that is new to them, they plan deliberately to develop strategies.
cards.limits: Applies only when the task is new or complex, which is why D4 has an applicability rule.

cards.finding: Leaders can raise people's confidence through persuasive communication, which may include information about strategies for reaching the goal.

cards.finding: Situational constraints, which include missing information, tools, and help, are linked to lower performance. Role clarity is defined as knowing what is expected and how to do it.
cards.limits: Cross-sectional. Based on few studies for this stressor.

cards.finding: In workplace studies, feedback combined with task clarification and job aids gave consistent improvements.

cards.finding: In workplace studies, feedback combined with goal setting improved performance.

cards.locator: p.275, Moderator Analyses: Major Conclusions, 1st paragraph; p.278, Implications, 1st paragraph
cards.finding: The more feedback keeps attention on the task and away from the self, the stronger its benefit for performance.
cards.limits: Compares groups of studies; no separate workplace result.

cards.finding: Effects on performance were weaker when feedback included praise than when it did not.
cards.limits: Praise is a broad category in S3. The rubric scores praise that names what was done well as task-focused, and a workplace study links positive supervisor feedback to later performance (PF-F1-c). The rewriter must not remove task-specific praise; it may only turn praise about the person into praise about the work.

review_draft02.limits: Scoring person-level praise as self-focused and task-specific praise as task-focused is team judgment.

review.by: Claude, at the user's request (2026-10-19). Not reviewed by the team.
review.note: Reconciled with PF-F1-c (Su & Jiang) so the two cards do not pull the rewriter in opposite directions on praise.

cards.locator: p.4, Sample and procedure and Measures; p.5, Table 3
cards.finding: Employees who perceived positive feedback from their supervisor received higher supervisor-rated performance four weeks later.
cards.limits: Rates the supervisor's feedback in general, not single messages. Measured differently from S3's praise.

cards.finding: Employees who saw their appraisal feedback as more specific were more likely to accept it, and acceptance was linked to job satisfaction.

cards.locator: Study 1 results p.873 and p.876; Study 2 results p.879; discussion p.880
cards.setting: Field (restaurant chain, 3,149 crew and 223 shift managers)
cards.finding: Employees spoke up with improvement ideas more often when they saw their manager as open. Openness was the leader behavior most consistently tied to speaking up, and the link held ten months later after controlling for earlier voice.
cards.limits: Self-report perceptions only. Leader behaviors added about 6 percent of variance in Study 1 and 2 percent in Study 2. One low-wage service company (p.881). The authors note earlier survey studies found no such link (p.870).

review.by: Drafted by Claude from the full PDF; added at the user's request (2026-11-07). Not reviewed by the team.

cards.finding: Openness means the manager listens, is interested in ideas, gives them fair consideration, and at least sometimes acts on what was raised. The authors advise managers to listen without defensiveness and to explain why they did or did not act on input.
cards.limits: The advice is the authors' implication and was not tested in the study.

cards.finding: Employees speak up more when managers ask for input and consult them, because this signals that input is welcome. Employees hold back when they expect input not to be taken seriously or acted on.
cards.limits: Narrative review. Evidence that voice improves unit outcomes is described as limited (p.179, p.187). Voice can raise turnover when managers cannot respond to what is raised (McClean et al. 2013, cited p.188).

cards.locator: results pp.365 to 368, Tables 4 to 6; appendix p.382
cards.finding: Teams whose members felt safe to bring up problems and tough issues showed more learning behavior, such as asking for help, seeking feedback and discussing errors, and that behavior predicted performance as rated by people outside the team. Leader coaching was related to this sense of safety.
cards.limits: Cross-sectional, one company, 51 teams. The author says the construct is not yet separated from trust and the antecedent findings are tentative (p.378). Coaching was near significance (p = .06, Table 6).
